title: Valve trombone versus slide
summary: He played valve trombone on many Moten records; valves cut notes mechanically while slide players lip between positions, as in J.J. Johnson.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Well, when you talked one time though, that you played valve trombone.
With Benny Moten, a lot of his records. That picture you looking at? That's a valve trombone there and a guitar. Nobody knows but that's a valve trombone sitting there in that '29 picture.
You look at that picture where Basie's in the band?
Yeah. And you would -- but you wouldn't solo on that, would you?
No, I didn't do any solos. I could have, but I thought that the man supposed to solo would let him solo. He was the solo (inaudible).
But why is it then that, you know, the one which seems to me which the valve solos come out so differently than the slide?
Because it's the valves cutting the notes (inaudible) horns moving.

The only thing cut a note on the slide is your lip. Only thing. And lifting from one position up to another position with your lip. See, because that horn runs down in degrees and to get that over again, you go back down (inaudible) come back up high, then you come up high again. And as you come up, you can sound like --
Well, one other thing then. Now, when you get to somebody like J.J. Johnson and Be-bop, you're now getting a style which sounds almost like a valve trombone.
Well, what's the point with that when you're playing the slide?
Because they running up the positions up, you know, lipping up. They lip it up. What they doing, they lipping from one position up and that's why it sounds like a valve.
Well, I mean, it actually takes the sort of the character of the trombone right away, doesn't it?
The character of the slide trombone is gone.
